coverage: Covering roughly Nov 15–16, 2026. Compiled Monday, ET.
note: Nvidia is expected to report this week; Anthropic's IPO is also due.

items.headline: Jensen Huang weighs a return to Nvidia; futures jump, then chips slide
items.summary: Huang is discussing a comeback as Nvidia CEO with allies, the FT reported Sunday, shared by @aleabitoreddit. US futures rose on the report, @KobeissiLetter noted, with the Nasdaq 100 up 0.7%, but by Monday morning Nasdaq 100 futures had erased the gains and fallen more than 1% as chip stocks sold off, with $NVDA trading below $160. @jimcramer: if the comeback were for real, the stock would be higher. Nvidia reports earnings this week and Anthropic is set to IPO.
items.short: An FT report of a Huang comeback lifted futures; chips gave it all back by morning.

items.headline: Kuo: OpenAI and Anthropic TPU orders push Google's shipment visibility to 2029
items.summary: Per analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, quoted by @jukan05, combined 2028-2029 demand is about 12M TPU units for OpenAI (designed by MediaTek) and about 14M for Anthropic (designed by Broadcom). Kuo puts realistic shipments at 8-9M, 14-15M and 16-18M units for 2027-2029, still growing in 2029 even though the market broadly expects AI capex to peak in 2028.
items.short: Kuo sees TPU shipments still rising in 2029 on OpenAI and Anthropic orders.

items.headline: Musk: Starship V4 grows about 40% longer, with nine engines
items.summary: Starship V4 will be about 70 m long, roughly a 40% length increase that allows more than 60% more propellant, @elonmusk posted. Engine count rises to nine, adding three more Raptor-Vacuum engines, all higher-thrust V4 engines.
items.short: A longer Starship with three more vacuum engines.

quoted.author: Melvin
quoted.text:
According to Korean media, foreign investors made a HUGE split between Korea's two memory giants this week.

From November 9 to 13, foreigners bought a net 1.70 trillion won of Samsung Electronics, about $1.2 billion.

Over the same five days, they sold a net 1.14 trillion won of SK Hynix, about $840 million.

That is a 2.84 trillion won swing between two companies that are riding the exact same memory boom.

I think this is foreign money rotating into the name that has more catching up to do.

SK Hynix has been the HBM leader for two years, while Samsung is just now proving itself with HBM4 and is pouring tens of trillions of won into new HBM capacity.

I don't think this is a bearish call on SK Hynix but rather a bet that Samsung is the bigger upside story from here.

items.author: Ren
items.text:
$NBIS $MU $LITE $AMD $ARM $NVDA

Can a Santa rally come early for tech? 

This is the worst tech momentum crash in more than 25 years.

Jefferies' tech momentum basket just fell 57% in 60 days. Not even the dot-com bust was as bad, it fell around -39%, the financial crisis at -31%.

With such a momentum crash, valuations reseted. We have given back all the bull run from March to June.

The S&P 500 went from 22.2x forward earnings in January to 18.3x today. That's below its 5-year average of 19.8x all the while earning estimates kept climbing the whole way down: +33% this year and +16% next year.

Hedge funds already made their yearly bonuses and sold, they made their biggest leverage cut since 2020 and are now net underweight AI for the first time since 2023. 

JPMorgan calls sentiment this bad a buy signal, I know you can’t just take their word at face value but when valuations hit such distressed levels, it’s really hard to ignore.

When everyone who wanted out is already out, there aren't many sellers left. I believe we're bound for a rebound, and I'd rather be early than chase it.

items.author: Daniel
items.text:
$CRWV is reportedly raising $4B at an interest rate of approximately 7.5%, backed by its $META contract.

This has absolutely nothing to do with the 16% yield on its unsecured bonds, which sent the market into a panic.

Investors acted as if CoreWeave would have to pay 16% to finance its expansion.

That’s complete nonsense.

CoreWeave’s actual cost of debt is declining.

CEO Michael Intrator made this crystal clear:

“At the end of Q3, our weighted average cost of debt across our entire business was 7.9%, down 250 basis points year-over-year.”

And he added:

“We will not use the unsecured debt market to fund our business at current yields, nor do we need to.”

The entire narrative that neoclouds are running out of financing options is absurd.

These companies have multiple ways to finance their expansion:

• GPU-backed debt.
• Debt backed by contracts with investment-grade customers.
• Data center-backed financing.
• Customer prepayments covering an increasingly large percentage of CapEx.

They don’t need to rely on expensive unsecured debt to fund their growth.

Yet investors have convinced themselves that neoclouds are heading toward a financing crisis.

$NBIS, $CRWV, and $IREN have all lost more than 50% of their market capitalizations from their peaks.

The market is treating a financing crisis as inevitable while these companies continue securing billions in capital.

Investors are dumping some of the fastest-growing companies in the world because they don’t understand how their expansion is financed.

This is an enormous opportunity.

And I’m buying.

items.title: The Spartan Secret to Staying Calm Under Pressure
items.author: Chris Williamson
items.summary: Drawing on Plutarch's line that Spartans were the only men for whom war brought a respite from training, the piece argues that the best cure for nerves is preparation so demanding that performance feels like rest. Breathwork and reframing help, it says, but hard work doesn't make a challenge easier; it makes it familiar. The closing advice: if you're scared, try working harder.

items.title: What an Enterprise Buyer Thinks About Nebius
items.author: M. V. Cunha
items.summary: A conversation with a Fortune 500 medtech AI-platform lead who buys from Nebius. His point: for regulated enterprises the binding constraint is often data gravity, not GPU supply, since governed data can't simply move to wherever compute is cheapest. He also warns that inference spend inside platforms like Snowflake Cortex and Databricks compounds quietly into a 'cost wall', which is where a full-stack offering like Token Factory could stand out.

items.title: Four Cards
items.rule: If a card is red on one side, it has a circle on the other.
items.explanation: Red could hide something that breaks the rule; Triangle breaks it if the other side turns out to be Red. Circle can't break it (the rule never says only those cards have it), and Blue isn't covered by the rule at all. Most people pick the card that matches the rule's second half instead of the one that could falsify it.
